opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it gets at something we often overlook when we talk about continual learning.

The way I think about it, a model that truly learns continually can't be in "online mode" all the time. When you're interacting with the world, processing tokens, solving tasks, your fast-updating memory systems are absorbing a lot of information. But that information is noisy, highly contextual, and often redundant. If you try to push all of it directly into the slow, persistent parameters, you get interference, which is essentially catastrophic forgetting. If you never push any of it, then nothing you learn in context really survives.

So sleep, or what we might call an offline consolidation phase, is the bridge between those two timescales. This connects naturally to how I think about memory more generally. In work like Titans and later Nested Learning, the idea is that a model isn't one monolithic set of weights with a single learning rate. It's a hierarchy of components, each updating at its own frequency. Some levels change every token, some change over longer spans, and some barely change at all. Sleep time is when you have the opportunity to move knowledge between those levels deliberately, rather than as a side effect of whatever data happens to be streaming in.

Neuroscience has an interesting parallel here. During sleep, the brain seems to replay recent experiences and gradually integrate them into longer-term cortical memory. That replay isn't a faithful recording. It's compressed, selective, and recombined, so the system extracts structure rather than memorizing episodes. I think a continual-learning model needs something similar. You'd want it to revisit what it encountered, decide what's surprising or important enough to keep, figure out how that relates to what it already knows, and then update the slower parameters in a way that preserves old capabilities.

There's also a computational argument. During inference you're latency-constrained and can only afford cheap updates. Offline, you can spend much more compute per piece of information. You can rehearse, generate your own variations, check consistency, and essentially think about what you've learned. So sleep time is partly a compute-allocation idea. It's when the model gets to do the expensive learning it couldn't afford in the moment.

I'll be honest, though: we're still early. We have good intuitions and some promising architectural ingredients, but we don't yet have a principled answer to questions like how often a model should sleep, what exactly it should replay, or how to measure whether consolidation helped versus quietly erased something. To me, those are among the most interesting open problems if we want models that keep getting better after deployment instead of being frozen snapshots.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes online interaction from offline consolidation, rather than saying training and test time have no distinction.

r002.rationale: It describes offline sleep as a chance to rehearse, generate variations, and do more expensive learning without relying on data streaming in.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think sleep is actually a really useful lens, and it's one of the things that motivated a lot of the work we've been doing on Titans and on the nested learning framework.

If you look at how biological systems handle continual learning, they don't do everything online in one shot. During the day, you're taking in a huge stream of experience, and most of it is being written into a fast, high-plasticity system, something like the hippocampus. You can't afford to reorganize your entire cortex every time you see a new fact, because you'd destroy everything you already know. That's catastrophic forgetting, basically. So the fast system absorbs the stream, and then sleep is the period where you consolidate: you replay, you compress, you decide what's worth moving into the slower, more stable memory, and you discard the rest.

For a model, I think of it in almost exactly those terms. In a truly continual-learning system you need at least two timescales. You have an online memory that's updating at test time, on every token or every chunk, with a fairly aggressive learning rate, and its job is to be surprised. It's tracking what's new, what violates the model's current expectations, and it stores that. Then you need a slower process, and this is the sleep-time analog, where you take what the fast memory has accumulated and you consolidate it into the parameters that persist, the long-term knowledge. Nested learning is really about formalizing that: you have optimization problems nested inside each other, each with its own update frequency, and the slow levels learn from the fast levels rather than from raw data.

What's interesting is that sleep time also solves a compute problem, not just a stability problem. You can't do expensive consolidation while you're serving requests. So the natural design is: during the "waking" phase the model is cheap and reactive, and during the "sleep" phase you can afford to do something heavier, replay the memory, run more gradient steps, maybe even restructure what's stored. And the forgetting mechanism matters just as much as the writing mechanism. A good sleep phase isn't just moving things from fast to slow, it's also deciding what to let go of, because memory capacity is finite and most of what you saw today isn't worth keeping.

So the short version is: I think sleep is where the actual learning happens. The waking phase is about capturing surprise, and the sleep phase is about turning surprise into knowledge without breaking the model.

r001.rationale: The response describes separate waking and sleep phases and says online memory updates at test time, but does not state that training time and test time are indistinguishable.

r002.rationale: It describes internal replay and gradient steps during sleep, but does not clearly say this improvement occurs while the model receives no external input.

astra-6.text:
I think sleep is a useful way to think about separating two parts of continual learning. While you’re interacting with the world, you need to absorb new information quickly, but you don’t necessarily want every experience to immediately change everything you’ve learned before. Then you need an opportunity to revisit those experiences, consolidate what matters, and integrate it with your existing knowledge.

So, for a model, sleep time could be a period where it’s not receiving new input but is still learning—replaying experiences, reorganizing memory, or updating components that change on a slower timescale. The important distinction is that being offline doesn’t mean learning has stopped.

I wouldn’t say a truly continual-learning model must sleep in exactly the biological sense. You could have consolidation happening in the background. What matters is having a mechanism that lets the model learn from the present without continually destroying its past. Sleep is one way to organize that process.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes interaction with the world from an offline consolidation period, but never states that training time and test time have no distinction.

r002.rationale: It says sleep time is a period with no new input where the model continues learning through replay, memory reorganization, or slower-timescale updates.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of sleep time as an opportunity for consolidation. In a continual-learning model, you’re constantly receiving new information, but incorporating something quickly and integrating it into what you already know are different problems. You want to learn from the current experience without overwriting useful knowledge from the past.

So the model could have an active phase where it interacts with the world and updates a relatively fast memory, and then a sleep phase where it revisits those experiences and integrates them into more persistent memory. That could involve replay, compression, or reorganizing what it has learned.

The important thing is that sleep doesn’t mean learning stops. It means the learning process changes. The model has an opportunity to work on its own accumulated experience instead of responding to another incoming observation. Whether that needs to be a distinct phase or can happen continuously in the background is an architectural question.

r001.rationale: It describes active and sleep phases but does not state that training time and test time have no distinction.

r002.rationale: It says that during sleep the model works on accumulated experience through replay, compression, or reorganization instead of responding to incoming observations.
